html:
A great irrigation canal of the Sasanian Empire in central Iraq, dug in the 6th century and traditionally credited to Shah Khosrow I. It ran for a great distance along the east side of the Tigris, taking water from the river north of Samarra and feeding the plains of the lower Diyala.

It turned a dry strip into one of the richest farming areas of Mesopotamia, dotted with villages and estates. It reached its peak under the Abbasid Caliphate, when it fed the land that supplied Baghdad, which lay near its course. A famous battle of 658, the Battle of Nahrawan between the caliph Ali and the Kharijites, took its name from the canal.

From the 10th century, war, weak government and failed repairs let the system decay. Breaches went unmended and silt filled the channels, and by the 12th century it was largely abandoned. Its ruin was one sign of the long decline of Iraq's farmland after the Abbasid golden age.
